items.prompt: An order service requires multi-row transactions, joins across normalized entities, and foreign-key constraints. Which data model is the starting point?
constraints: Joins are part of the access contract.

options.text: Evaluate a relational database and size its transaction, connection, storage, and read or write workload from measured access patterns.
Use a key-value store and reconstruct every join in application memory without modeling consistency.
Use object storage as the transactional order database.
Use a cache as the only source of order truth.

feedback.Reason: Relational semantics fit transactions, joins, and declarative integrity requirements.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Relational engines provide transactions, SQL joins, constraints, and indexed access patterns.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses an engine and sizes connections, storage, IOPS, replicas, and failover from the workload.
Details.errorCorrection: Application joins increase complexity and can weaken atomicity, S3 is object storage, and caches are not authoritative.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Relational scale and schema constraints may require sharding or a purpose-built service at extreme scale.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Application joins do not automatically preserve multi-row transactional integrity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Object storage does not provide order transactions or joins.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Caches can lose or stale data and cannot be the system of record.

items.prompt: A session service performs point reads and writes by a unique session ID, with no joins and predictable key access. Which model should be compared?

options.text: Evaluate a key-value database such as DynamoDB, designing partition keys, item size, consistency, capacity, and expiration behavior.
Choose a relational database solely because every workload uses tables.
Use a graph database because sessions have a unique key.
Use a read cache without a durable session store.

feedback.Reason: Predictable point access without joins is a strong key-value workload signal.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB partitions data by key and provides managed low-latency access with configured capacity and consistency choices.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner checks key distribution, item growth, TTL, hot-key risk, and session loss behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Relational is possible but may add unnecessary operational shape, graph is a different relationship model, and cache alone is not durable.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Key-value scale requires access-pattern discipline and can make ad hoc queries harder.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Relational tables are not required when the access pattern is simple key lookup.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A unique key does not create a graph relationship workload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache can expire or be lost and should not be the only session authority when durability is required.

items.prompt: A product catalog has variable attributes by product type and is read as a complete product aggregate. Which model is a candidate?
constraints: The aggregate is usually read together.

options.text: Evaluate a document model such as DynamoDB item aggregates, designing access keys, item size, update patterns, and secondary indexes.
Normalize every attribute into many relational tables despite aggregate access and variable shape.
Use a graph store because attributes are optional.
Use a CDN as the catalog source of truth.

feedback.Reason: Document-style aggregates fit variable attributes that are accessed together.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB items can hold flexible attributes and are modeled around known access patterns and item boundaries.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect checks item size, update contention, key design, and index cost before choosing the aggregate shape.
Details.errorCorrection: Relational normalization can add joins and write complexity, graph is not implied by optional fields, and CDN data is a cache.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Denormalization simplifies reads but duplicates data and makes cross-aggregate queries harder.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Normalized tables are not automatically best for aggregate reads and variable shape.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Optional attributes do not imply graph traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A CDN cannot be the authoritative catalog database.

items.prompt: A fraud service must traverse relationships among accounts, devices, and transactions across multiple hops. Which data model should be evaluated?
constraints: The graph is operational, not only analytical.

options.text: Evaluate a graph database such as Neptune, modeling vertices, edges, traversal latency, consistency, and write or read scaling.
Use a key-value table and scan all entities for every multi-hop query.
Use a relational schema without indexes or join-performance testing.
Use S3 object prefixes as a graph traversal engine.

feedback.Reason: Graph traversal and relationship-centric access are a distinct database signal.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Amazon Neptune provides graph models and traversal engines for relationship data.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner benchmarks traversal depth, write consistency, query patterns, and data volume against the risk model.
Details.errorCorrection: Scans and unindexed joins do not provide predictable traversal, S3 prefixes are object organization, and relational remains possible only with measured fit.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Graph models optimize relationships but add specialized query and operational skills.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Full scans are not a scalable multi-hop access pattern.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Unindexed relational joins can miss latency requirements.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object prefixes do not execute graph traversals.

items.prompt: A telemetry service ingests timestamped measurements at high write rate and queries recent time windows and aggregates. Which store should be compared?

options.text: Evaluate a time-series database such as Timestream, modeling time dimensions, retention, memory or magnetic tiers, and query workload.
Use a relational database with one unindexed table for unlimited telemetry.
Use a key-value store without a time or partition strategy.
Use a cache as the only telemetry history.

feedback.Reason: Timestamped ingestion and windowed queries are a time-series workload signal.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Amazon Timestream is designed for time-series ingestion, retention tiers, and temporal queries.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect defines dimensions, measure cardinality, retention, late data, and query latency.
Details.errorCorrection: Unindexed relational tables grow poorly, key-value needs an explicit time model, and caches do not retain durable history.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Purpose-built time-series storage simplifies temporal access but constrains query and migration patterns.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: An unindexed growing table is not a measured scalable design.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Key-value can work only with a deliberate time and partition model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache is not durable telemetry history.

items.prompt: A workload writes very large ordered datasets by partition and scans selected partitions in parallel. Which database pattern should be evaluated?

options.text: Evaluate a wide-column or partition-oriented database such as Amazon Keyspaces, designing partition key, clustering, throughput, and hotspot behavior.
Use a single relational table with one hot sequential key.
Use a graph database because partitions are relationships.
Use object storage without a query or partition strategy.

feedback.Reason: Partition-oriented wide-column access fits high-scale writes and known partition reads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Amazon Keyspaces uses a Cassandra-compatible wide-column model whose partition key and clustering design drive scale and access.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner distributes partitions, measures request units and latency, and avoids hot keys or unbounded partitions.
Details.errorCorrection: A single relational hot key limits scale, graph does not follow from partitioning, and object storage needs an analytical access layer.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Wide-column scale requires query-driven schema and limits ad hoc relational access.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A hot sequential key concentrates writes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object storage alone does not provide the required operational query model.

items.prompt: A payment authorization read must immediately observe a just-committed write, while product browsing can tolerate stale reads. What should the model capture?
constraints: The payment path has a correctness requirement.
Read and write paths are separable.

options.text: Model consistency per access path, use the strongest supported read or transaction semantics for authorization, and allow weaker reads only where product behavior permits.
Use eventual consistency for every read because it is always faster and safe.
Use a cache for authorization without invalidation or version checks.
Duplicate writes to unrelated databases without a commit or reconciliation strategy.

feedback.Reason: Consistency is an access-pattern and business-correctness requirement, not a single database-wide slogan.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS databases expose different consistency, transaction, and replica-read options with latency trade-offs.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect makes authorization reads strongly consistent or transactionally bounded and keeps browse reads cost-efficient.
Details.errorCorrection: Eventual reads can violate payment correctness, caches need invalidation or versioning, and dual writes can diverge.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Strong consistency can add latency, capacity, or cost and should be limited to required paths.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Some business paths cannot tolerate stale data.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Authorization caching without freshness control can permit invalid decisions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Independent writes need a distributed consistency or reconciliation design.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB workload has a small set of popular keys and throttles despite adequate table capacity. What access-pattern issue is likely?
constraints: Total table demand is below provisioned capacity.
The application can change key design.

options.text: Investigate hot partitions and redesign or shard the access key where semantics permit, then validate item reads, writes, and fan-out cost.
Increase table capacity without checking partition distribution.
Add a relational join to distribute DynamoDB keys.
Put the hot item in a cache and leave all writes on one key without invalidation.

feedback.Reason: DynamoDB capacity is partitioned and a hot key can throttle even when aggregate capacity appears sufficient.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Partition-key distribution determines where item traffic lands; write or read sharding can spread a hot logical key.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures per-key demand, chooses a deterministic shard strategy, and handles fan-out or aggregation correctly.
Details.errorCorrection: More aggregate capacity may not fix a hot partition, joins are not DynamoDB partitioning, and cache-only writes create stale or lost state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Sharding improves distribution but complicates reads, writes, and key management.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Aggregate capacity does not guarantee a hot partition can absorb demand.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Relational joins do not distribute DynamoDB partition traffic.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Caching a hot read does not solve write concentration or invalidation.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB query requires an alternate access pattern by status and time, but a table scan is too slow. What should be considered?
constraints: The indexed projection can be defined.

options.text: Evaluate a global or local secondary index with a distributed key and projected attributes, measuring write amplification, storage, and query latency.
Use a full table scan for every request.
Create an index with a single constant partition key for all items.
Use a cache without a refresh or correctness policy.

feedback.Reason: A known alternate access pattern should be represented by an index or deliberately redesigned query model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB secondary indexes provide alternate key access but consume storage and write capacity and can hotspot.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect distributes index keys, projects only needed fields, and validates index lag or consistency for the use case.
Details.errorCorrection: Scans do not scale for request paths, constant keys hotspot, and caches need freshness semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Indexes simplify reads but increase write and storage cost and add another partitioned capacity path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Per-request scans have poor latency and cost at scale.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A constant partition key creates a hot index partition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Caching without freshness rules can return incorrect status data.

items.prompt: An event service appends immutable events and reads streams by aggregate ID and sequence. Which modeling principle matters?

options.text: Choose a partition and sort-key model or purpose-built stream store that preserves aggregate ordering, distributes writes, and supports replay and retention.
Update one mutable row for every event and discard event history.
Use a random partition key that makes ordered reads impossible.
Use a cache as the only event log.

feedback.Reason: Immutable append workloads need an ordered, durable, replayable access model.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Partition and sort keys or streaming services can represent aggregate order while distributing independent streams.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses retention, sequence, replay, duplicate, and hot-aggregate behavior before implementation.
Details.errorCorrection: Mutable rows lose history, random keys break ordering, and caches are not durable logs.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Ordering scope must be limited because global order reduces scalability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Overwriting events prevents replay and audit history.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: An unordered key cannot support the stated sequence access.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cache eviction or failure loses the event log.

items.prompt: A product team needs frequent ad hoc joins, filters, and reporting queries that change weekly. Which model is more suitable than a fixed key-value schema?
constraints: The workload is operational or mixed.

options.text: Evaluate a relational or analytical database with indexes, query planning, and workload isolation rather than forcing every query into a fixed key design.
Use a key-value store and scan every item for each new question.
Use a cache because ad hoc queries are always temporary.
Use object prefixes as a general SQL optimizer.

feedback.Reason: Changing joins and filters need a query model that does not require a new key schema for every question.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Relational and analytical engines provide SQL, indexes, statistics, and query plans for flexible access.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect separates operational and analytical workloads, sizes connections and storage, and validates query concurrency.
Details.errorCorrection: Key-value scans are inefficient, caches are not authoritative query stores, and object prefixes do not optimize joins.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Flexible queries can cost more compute and require indexing or workload governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Scans undermine predictable performance at scale.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A cache cannot replace durable flexible query execution.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object organization is not a relational query optimizer.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB table uses a low-cardinality partition key such as country and throttles one country during peak traffic. What should change?
constraints: The partition key is low cardinality.
The access pattern can add a shard or finer key.

options.text: Use a higher-cardinality or deliberately sharded partition key that distributes the hot country while preserving the required query access.
Increase table capacity without changing the concentrated key.
Use the country value as a sort key under one constant partition.
Disable throttling errors so clients continue writing.

feedback.Reason: Low-cardinality keys concentrate traffic and can create hot partitions.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB partitions by partition key; adding entropy or write sharding spreads high-volume logical groups.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner chooses deterministic shard suffixes, handles read fan-out, and migrates existing data safely.
Details.errorCorrection: More capacity cannot always fix a hot partition, sort key under one partition remains concentrated, and hiding errors loses data.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Finer partitioning complicates queries and aggregation but improves horizontal distribution.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: The bottleneck can be one partition rather than total table capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A sort key does not distribute items across partitions under a single partition key.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Errors must remain visible and handled.

items.prompt: A document workload adds optional attributes frequently, while old readers must continue to work. Which design characteristic is useful?

options.text: Use an evolvable document or item model with versioned validation, backward-compatible readers, and migration for fields whose semantics cannot remain implicit.
Change every item atomically before deploying any compatible reader.
Assume flexible schema removes the need for data contracts.
Store new attributes in a separate cache with no durable migration.

feedback.Reason: Flexible schema helps additive evolution but does not remove contracts, validation, or migration needs.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Document stores permit variable attributes, while application versions and critical field semantics still require coordination.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner adds version markers, supports old readers, and migrates data when access or validation requires it.
Details.errorCorrection: Atomic fleet-wide rewrites increase migration risk, flexible schema is not contract-free, and cache state is not durable migration.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Schema flexibility speeds evolution but can create inconsistent shapes and validation burden.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Reader compatibility should precede data transformation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Flexible fields still need ownership, types, and lifecycle rules.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache cannot be the authoritative schema migration store.

items.prompt: A large data set is written once and scanned repeatedly for analytical aggregates, without low-latency transactional updates. Which service class should be compared?
constraints: Data can be loaded in batches.
Interactive transaction latency is not primary.

options.text: Evaluate an analytical store such as Athena or Redshift with columnar, partition, compression, concurrency, and data-lifecycle choices modeled.
Use the transactional primary database for every large scan without workload isolation.
Use a key-value lookup for full-table aggregates.
Use an application cache as the analytical source of truth.

feedback.Reason: Batch scans and aggregates are analytical access patterns and should be isolated from transactional workloads.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Athena and Redshift optimize different analytical storage and query patterns over data lakes or warehouses.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect partitions data, chooses file format and workgroup or cluster capacity, and protects operational databases.
Details.errorCorrection: Large scans can starve transactions, key-value is not a scan engine, and caches are not durable analytical stores.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Analytical services add data pipeline and query governance but protect operational latency.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Mixed scans can consume transactional CPU, I/O, and connections.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Point lookup models are not analytical scans.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A cache does not replace a durable analytical dataset and query engine.

items.prompt: A session and temporary-token store should remove expired items without a scheduled full-table cleanup. Which database feature should be evaluated?
constraints: Expired data can be removed eventually.
The application does not require exact deletion time.

options.text: Use a supported TTL or expiration mechanism and design reads to tolerate eventual removal and stale expired items until the service deletes them.
Assume TTL deletion is an exact-time transaction for every request.
Use a database scan every second for all expired rows.
Use a cache eviction policy as the durable token-expiration contract.

feedback.Reason: TTL reduces cleanup work but has service-specific eventual deletion semantics.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB TTL marks expired items for background deletion rather than an exact-time synchronous transaction.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner stores expiry, rejects expired items at read time where necessary, and monitors storage and deletion behavior.
Details.errorCorrection: Exact-time deletion cannot be assumed, scans are expensive, and cache eviction is not a durable database contract.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: TTL simplifies retention but leaves a window of storage and read-state behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: TTL removal is asynchronous and needs application-side expiry checks when correctness matters.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Frequent scans waste capacity and scale poorly.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cache eviction is not the authoritative token state.

items.prompt: A service needs atomic updates within one aggregate but not across unrelated customers. What modeling choice can improve scale?

options.text: Align the partition or transaction boundary with the aggregate so writes remain atomic locally while independent aggregates scale separately.
Use one global transaction for every customer to simplify correctness.
Remove transactions and rely on eventual repair for payment state.
Use a cache to coordinate atomic writes across all aggregates.

feedback.Reason: Bounded transaction scope can preserve required atomicity while avoiding an unnecessary global coordination bottleneck.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Relational and NoSQL designs scale better when ownership and transaction boundaries match the business aggregate.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect states invariants, uses conditional or transactional writes for the aggregate, and uses workflows for cross-aggregate effects.
Details.errorCorrection: Global transactions reduce scale, removing payment transactions risks inconsistency, and caches cannot guarantee atomic durable state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Local atomicity may require asynchronous coordination and reconciliation across aggregates.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Global transaction scope creates contention and limits scale.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Eventual repair cannot replace an invariant that must hold at commit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Caches do not provide durable cross-aggregate transactions.

items.prompt: A high-volume ingestion service writes independent records and can retry batches. Which access pattern should be optimized?

options.text: Use batched writes where supported, partition keys evenly, handle unprocessed items with backoff, and make retries idempotent.
Send one synchronous transaction for every record regardless of independence.
Retry unprocessed items in a tight loop without backoff.
Use one partition key to keep the batch ordered.

feedback.Reason: Independent high-volume writes benefit from batching and evenly distributed keys with bounded retry.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB batch APIs return unprocessed items and require application retry behavior; partition distribution controls capacity.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner batches within service limits, backs off, logs failures, and uses deterministic record keys.
Details.errorCorrection: Per-record sync adds overhead, tight retry loops amplify throttling, and one key creates a hot partition.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Batching improves efficiency but requires partial-failure handling and ordering assumptions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Independent records do not require a transaction per item and incur more overhead.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Backoff protects the service and improves eventual success.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: One key concentrates traffic and is not a safe scale strategy.

items.prompt: A single application has transactional orders, graph fraud queries, time-series telemetry, and analytical scans. What architecture is safer than forcing one engine to do all work?
constraints: Data ownership and synchronization are explicit.

options.text: Use purpose-built stores or separated analytical paths where each access pattern justifies it, with explicit data ownership, ingestion, consistency, and operational boundaries.
Use one database for every workload regardless of access pattern.
Replicate every write synchronously to all engines without a failure or cost model.
Use caches as the common durable integration layer.

feedback.Reason: Distinct access patterns can justify purpose-built services when synchronization and operations are designed explicitly.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS offers relational, key-value, graph, time-series, and analytical stores with different performance contracts.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses one authoritative owner per fact, uses events or pipelines for derived views, and tests lag and recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: One engine can become a compromise bottleneck, synchronous fan-out increases failure and cost, and caches are not durable integration stores.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multiple stores improve fit but add data movement, schema, monitoring, and recovery work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A single engine may force poor performance or semantics across incompatible paths.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Synchronous multi-engine writes create availability and consistency coupling.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Caches are not durable system-of-record integration layers.

items.prompt: A database choice is proposed from product names without documenting reads, writes, consistency, joins, cardinality, growth, or recovery. What should the architect require?
constraints: Workload measurements are available or can be collected.
The service has an availability target.

options.text: Document access patterns, transaction and consistency needs, data shape, partition or index behavior, latency, scale, protection, cost, and operating model before selecting the engine.
Choose the database with the highest advertised throughput.
Choose the cheapest storage price without modeling requests or backups.
Choose the most familiar engine and defer workload profiling until production.

feedback.Reason: Database selection is driven by the workload contract and failure model, not a product label or one benchmark.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Engine semantics, access paths, limits, replicas, storage, throughput, and recovery determine system behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner measures representative traffic, selects one canonical service, and validates migration, backup, and failover.
Details.errorCorrection: Peak specifications can be irrelevant, storage price omits request and protection costs, and familiarity is not fit evidence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Profiling takes time but prevents schema and service choices that are expensive to replace.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Advertised maximum throughput may not match the access pattern or consistency mode.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Requests, capacity, backups, and recovery add material cost dimensions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Unprofiled production selection creates avoidable performance and migration risk.
